title: Operational identifiability of false-vacuum decay rates in the quantum Ising chain
authors: Boliang Yu, Ruixin Zhou, Hang Su
abstract: Extracting a thermodynamic nucleation rate from finite-time quantum dynamics requires separating observable decay from estimator and finite-size validity. We develop a multilevel identification framework to real-time tensor-network simulations of false-vacuum decay in the one-dimensional quantum Ising chain. Across twelve parameter points with non-empty analysis intervals, the same coherent two-kink amplitudes semi-quantitatively predict both infinite-chain survival and magnetization dynamics: the survival coefficient has a median lattice-to-theory ratio of 0.902, while the magnetization-area slope ratios span 0.809--0.953. By contrast, the microscopic nearest-neighbour bond response is coherence dominated: vacuum--pair coherence contributes 60.0--81.5\% within the seven parameter points satisfying the matched-bond-dimension convergence criterion, while substantial late-window slope discrepancies remain that cannot be removed by a scalar normalization. The framework establishes reliable finite-time decay coefficients and identifies the additional finite-size and branch-validation requirements for a bulk thermodynamic rate interpretation. Within the two-kink model, a lattice-resolved WKB action reduces the median fixed-prefactor discrepancy with the coherent-bubble spectral calculation to 4.13\%. Quantitative cross-level consistency, observable-dependent reduced-model error, and a thermodynamic-rate interpretation that remains subject to finite-size validation can therefore coexist.
summary: This paper tackles the difficult problem of determining a true, bulk thermodynamic decay rate from limited, finite-time quantum simulation data on the Ising chain. The authors introduce a robust multilevel framework that successfully cross-validates results across different theoretical approximations. While they establish strong consistency evidence, they conclude that further computational work on size extrapolation is required to claim a definitive thermodynamic result.
main_problem: The core challenge is establishing an operational link between finite-time quantum dynamics simulations and a true, bulk thermodynamic false-vacuum decay rate.
main_result: A multilevel identification framework was developed showing quantitative consistency across different theoretical levels (L0 to L2), but the final interpretation of a bulk rate remains conditional on performing necessary future size-extrapolation tests.
method: The authors use real-time tensor-network simulations combined with multi-level analysis, comparing observables derived from finite time windows against predictions from coherent-bubble theory and semiclassical WKB actions.
model_or_system: The system is the one-dimensional quantum Ising chain governed by a Hamiltonian involving transverse ($\sigma_x$) and longitudinal ($\sigma_z$) fields. The study focuses on the dynamics of false-vacuum decay in this model.
key_observables: Survival coefficient, magnetization dynamics, vacuum–pair coherence contribution, lattice-resolved WKB action discrepancy, and various correlation readouts ($R1$ through $R4$).
important_parameters: Transverse field ($h^\perp$), longitudinal field ($h_\parallel$), system size ($L$), and the comparison between finite-time vs. infinite-chain limits.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that consistency across multiple theoretical levels (e.g., L0 matching L1) provides strong evidence, but it explicitly notes these are not sufficient proof for a full thermodynamic rate without further size validation.
figures_summary: Figures compare rates derived from different actions and show the quantitative agreement between iMPS survival coefficients and coherent-bubble slopes across various parameter points.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first defining the identifiability problem, developing a multilevel framework comparing lattice observables (L0) to spectral theory (L1) and semiclassical limits (L2), establishing consistency checks through multiple readouts, and finally concluding with the necessary next steps for full thermodynamic validation.
why_interesting: The rigorous methodology for extracting bulk properties from finite-time quantum simulations is highly relevant to open quantum systems and non-equilibrium dynamics in condensed matter theory.
